In Emerging Tech, the Only Strategy Question Is Which Bets You Can Take Back.

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 2 August 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

In short: Companies in emerging categories are told two contradictory things: move fast, because the window is closing, and be careful, because the rules are still being written. Both are true. The way to hold them together is not a balance between speed and caution. It is a sorting rule: which decisions can be taken back, and which cannot. Reversible decisions should be made quickly, cheaply and in parallel. Irreversible ones should be made slowly, one at a time, after the reversible ones have produced evidence.

Key points

  • A reversible decision costs a bounded amount if wrong and lets the company return to roughly where it started. An irreversible one changes what the company is.
  • Emerging-tech companies fail by treating irreversible decisions as reversible, and reversible ones with the slowness the irreversible deserve.
  • Public claims are irreversible: US regulators have fined companies for AI capabilities they did not have, and the record stays public.
  • Some irreversibility is legal fact: after the EU's MiCA transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, unauthorised crypto-asset service providers had to stop onboarding EU clients and wind down.
  • A one-page discipline sorts the quarter's ten decisions, gives each reversible one a test, a budget and a date, and names the evidence each irreversible one needs.

Two kinds of decision

A reversible decision is one where being wrong costs a bounded amount and the company can return to roughly where it started. A channel test. A pricing experiment. A partnership with a short term. A market segment tried for a quarter. A feature built behind a flag.

An irreversible decision is one where being wrong changes what the company is. A regulatory posture chosen before the rules are clear. A token launched. A category claimed publicly. A large client accepted at a share of revenue that makes the company dependent on it. A platform relied on as the only channel. A name filed as a trademark. Capital raised on a thesis the company will be held to.

The distinction is old and well tested. Jeff Bezos's 2016 letter to Amazon shareholders described many decisions as "reversible, two-way doors" that can use a lightweight process, and argued that most decisions "should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had."

Emerging-tech companies fail in a characteristic way: they treat irreversible decisions as if they were reversible, because everyone around them is moving fast, and they treat reversible decisions with a slowness that belongs to the irreversible ones, because the uncertainty makes everything feel weighty.

The rule

Reversible decisions should be made quickly, cheaply, and in parallel. Irreversible ones should be made slowly, expensively, and one at a time, after the reversible ones have produced evidence.

That is the same discipline we apply to distribution: observe cheaply in several places, commit completely to one. It generalises to company strategy because the underlying problem is the same. Uncertainty is high, information is expensive, and the cost of a wrong commitment is asymmetric. Our piece on GTM strategy versus tactics makes the distribution version of the argument.

Speed belongs to decisions you can take back, and care belongs to the ones you cannot.

Record the irreversible ones as you make them. A decision record with the reason, the owner, the evidence relied on and the expected outcome is what lets a company learn from a one-way door it has already walked through.

Applying it in AI

In AI, the reversible decisions are which buyer to serve first, which channels to test, which integrations to build, what to charge. The irreversible ones are which model providers to depend on, which data the product accumulates and under what terms, which claims about accuracy and safety the company makes in public, and which regulated use cases it enters.

The evidence shows why those four belong on the slow list.

Model dependency hardens over time. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 CIOs found agentic workflows were making it harder to switch between models, because the surrounding prompts, tools and checks are tuned to each. A model choice that was reversible at prototype stage becomes much less so once customers depend on the workflow. Menlo Ventures' 2026 data shows the supply side is not stable enough to bet on a single provider: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. Our guide to build versus buy for AI agents covers how to keep that door open.

Public claims do not come back. In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers for saying they used AI in ways they did not, with $400,000 in combined penalties. In September 2024 the FTC's Operation AI Comply targeted companies whose AI claims could not be substantiated. An enforcement record stays public long after the copy is corrected.

The rules move under you. The EU AI Act's stand-alone high-risk obligations under Annex III were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the amendments in Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. A company that rebuilt its product around the original timeline made a reasonable choice that turned out to be early. A company that entered a high-risk use case without a compliance plan made one that will be expensive to reverse. Our guide to the EU AI Act for commercial teams covers the current dates.

A company that spends its first year testing buyers and channels cheaply, while being deliberately slow about its data terms and public claims, will look less decisive than one that announced a category on day one. It will also still exist when the category's rules are written.

Applying it in Web3

In Web3, the reversibility line is unusually sharp, because so much is literally irreversible. A token, once distributed, cannot be un-distributed. A treasury decision made on-chain is public forever. A regulatory posture, once a product is live in a jurisdiction, is a fact the regulator has already observed.

The EU shows what that last point means in practice. ESMA's June 2026 statement on the end of MiCA's transitional period on 1 July 2026 told unauthorised crypto-asset service providers to stop onboarding new EU clients, stop marketing, restrict services to an orderly exit and tell clients repeatedly about wind-down timelines. A firm that treated its EU posture as something it could settle later found the decision had been made for it. Our piece on token or no token applies the same logic to the launch decision.

The reversible decisions, which audience to serve first, which distribution partners to try, which incentives to test at small scale, deserve speed. The irreversible ones deserve the slowest, most expensive process the company can afford, including advice the founders would rather not pay for.

DecisionReversible?Fast pathSlow path: evidence needed first
First buyer segmentYesTest two segments for a quarter eachNot needed
Channel mixYesSmall budgets in several channels, one ownerNot needed
Price pointMostlyPrice experiment with a review dateNot needed
Primary model providerBecomes less soRun the core workflow on a second modelCost, quality and switching time on both
Public accuracy or safety claimNoNoneA dated eval a buyer or regulator could check
Regulated use case or jurisdictionNoNoneLegal opinion, compliance plan, licence route
Token launchNoNoneUser demand without the token, legal review, distribution plan

Timing windows are real, and they are narrower than they look

Emerging categories have moments when decisions get made: budget cycles, regulatory clarity, a platform opening or closing a category, a competitor's failure, the weeks after a major model release. A company should know which windows matter to its buyers and prepare reversible experiments to run inside them.

But a window is a reason to be ready, not a reason to make an irreversible commitment in a hurry. The company that has already run its cheap tests enters the window with evidence. The company that has not enters it with conviction, which is what a bet feels like from the inside.

A one-page strategy discipline

List the ten decisions in front of the company this quarter. Mark each reversible or irreversible. For the reversible ones, write the test, the budget, and the date. For the irreversible ones, write what evidence would have to exist before the decision is made, and which reversible decisions produce that evidence.

ColumnFor a reversible decisionFor an irreversible decision
OwnerOne named personOne named person, plus who must agree
Test or evidenceThe test and what result would change the planThe evidence that must exist before deciding
BudgetThe most it can cost if wrongThe cost of being wrong, written down
DateWhen the test reportsThe earliest date the evidence can exist
FeedsWhich irreversible decision this informsWhich reversible tests produce the evidence

Most companies discover that they have been arguing about the irreversible decisions and neglecting the reversible ones that would settle the argument.

In an emerging category, speed belongs to decisions you can take back and care belongs to the ones you cannot. Run the reversible tests first, and let them earn the irreversible commitment.

lowob takeaways

  • Sort before you debate. Mark every decision reversible or irreversible before arguing about it.
  • Move fast on the reversible. Audience, channels, small incentive tests and prices deserve speed and parallel tests.
  • Slow down on the irreversible. Model dependency, public claims, regulated entry and tokens deserve the slowest process the company can afford.
  • Let tests settle arguments. Most arguments about one-way doors are settled by two-way tests nobody has run.

Common questions

What is the difference between a reversible and an irreversible business decision?

A reversible decision costs a bounded amount if wrong and lets the company return to roughly where it started, such as a channel test or a price experiment. An irreversible one changes what the company is, such as a public claim, a token launch or a regulated market entry.

How should startups make decisions under uncertainty?

Make reversible decisions quickly, cheaply and in parallel, and irreversible ones slowly and one at a time, after the reversible tests have produced evidence. Write down, for each irreversible decision, what evidence must exist first.

Which AI startup decisions are hard to reverse?

Dependence on one model provider, the data the product accumulates and its terms, public accuracy and safety claims, and entry into regulated use cases. Switching models gets harder as agentic workflows are built around them.

Why is timing so important in emerging technology markets?

Categories have windows, such as budget cycles, regulatory clarity or a major model release. A window is a reason to have tests ready, not a reason to make an irreversible commitment in a hurry.

Sources and notes

  • Amazon, 2016 Letter to Shareholders, published 2017. Company letter; describes Amazon's practice, not a study.
  • US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence, 18 March 2024. Settled orders; the firms neither admitted nor denied the findings.
  • US Federal Trade Commission, FTC Announces Crackdown on Deceptive AI Claims and Schemes, 25 September 2024. Regulator press release; several cases were allegations at the time.
  • ESMA, Public statement on the end of the MiCA transitional period, 23 June 2026. Regulator statement; national authorities apply it.
  • Andreessen Horowitz, How 100 Enterprise CIOs Are Building and Buying Gen AI in 2025, 10 June 2025. Investor research; data as of May 2025.
  • Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 November 2026. Investor research; market shares are Menlo's spend estimates.
  • Gibson Dunn, EU AI Act Omnibus Agreement: Postponed High-Risk Deadlines and Other Key Changes, 2026. Law firm analysis of the agreement later adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
